cues.say: Component seventeen: hosted checkout and webhooks.
Hosted checkout is a pattern for taking payments. Customers pay on the payment provider's own page, not yours. The provider then calls your server, with a webhook, to say the payment worked.
With Stripe, that's Stripe Checkout. You never build a card form at all.
Why not build your own card form? Then card numbers pass through your servers, and maybe into your logs and database.
Anything that touches card numbers falls under PCI, the card industry's security rules. That means heavy audits for every server involved.
Instead, when the customer clicks pay, your server asks Stripe for a checkout session, with the order and amount. Stripe answers with a link.
The browser is redirected to Stripe's page, and the customer types their card there. The card number never touches your servers.
When the payment succeeds, Stripe calls your server. That's a webhook: the provider calling a web address of yours when something happens.
Why not just trust the redirect back to your site? The customer might close the tab first. The webhook comes either way.
Your webhook handler first checks the signature, proof the message came from Stripe. Then it saves the event's id.
It marks the order paid, and replies OK fast. Slow work, like texting the customer, goes on a queue for later.
Use it for every payment. Refunds and disputes arrive as webhooks too, so the same handler covers them.
Now a real case: order forty-two, twenty-four dollars, at the pizza shop. The server creates a checkout session, and the customer pays on Stripe's page.
Stripe sends the webhook: event one, order forty-two paid. The server marks it paid, and replies OK.
Later, the same event arrives again. Its id is already saved, so it's ignored. Without that check, the kitchen could cook the order twice.
Here's where it sits: the API talks to Stripe, the customer pays on Stripe's page, and the webhook comes back.
Two things to know. Webhooks can repeat and arrive late, so ignore known ids, and never assume their order.
And Stripe has rate limits, about a hundred requests a second by default. Ask for more before a big launch.
In the interview, say: card data never touches our servers, which shrinks our PCI scope.
